items.q: What's the difference between async/semi-sync/sync replication? What problems does replication lag cause?
items.a: - [[b:Async]]: primary commit returns immediately, replica applies later → has [[r:lag]] (reading from the replica shows stale data) - [[b:Semi-sync]]: primary waits for ≥1 replica ack before committing → reduces lag/increases durability, trades off write latency - [[b:Sync]]: waits for every replica → safest, slowest [[r:Lag consequence]]: 'I just transferred money, why hasn't my balance changed?' — from reading a lagging replica by mistake. :::deep Two kinds of lag: - [[b:apply lag]]: replica replays slowly - [[b:transport lag]]: network Measured with `Seconds_Behind_Master` (coarse) or a heartbeat table (more accurate). - [[r:Semi-sync trap]]: if the only ack-ing replica dies, the primary can *degrade to async* → thresholds and alerting must be configured - Aurora separates storage/compute → a 'replica' reads the same volume → millisecond lag (very different from binlog replication) OTA: 'history/loyalty' can read from a replica freely; 'wallet balance / just-created booking' must use [[g:read-your-writes]] back to the writer. :::

items.q: How do you guarantee read-after-write consistency when reading from a replica?
items.a:
- [[g:Read-your-writes]]: after a write, route that user's reads to the primary for a few seconds
- [[g:Version/LSN check]]: only read from a replica that has applied up to the user's commit position (Aurora supports this)
- [[g:Sticky/monotonic reads]]: keep the same replica as long as it's recent enough

:::tip Fintech
balances and core data read from the primary; only reports/older history/analytics get pushed to a replica.
:::

:::deep
- [[b:read-your-writes]]: route the just-written user's reads to the primary within a window of a few seconds (sticky by user/session)
- [[b:LSN/GTID gating]]: after writing, get the log position, and only read from a replica that has applied up to it (Aurora/Postgres)
- [[b:monotonic reads]]: use the same replica for one session so time doesn't 'go backwards'

[[r:Trap]]: a load balancer round-robins across replicas with different lag → the user sees data jump around.

Rule: data the user expects to see immediately after writing → primary.
:::

items.q: Master-slave vs multi-master — what's the trade-off?
items.a:
Single-primaryMulti-master
Writes1 placemultiple places
Write conflictnonemust be resolved (LWW/CRDT/app)
Weaknessbottleneck + SPOF (needs failover)complex, easy to lose consistency
Good formost systems (especially ledgers)high-availability multi-region
Fintech [[r:rarely uses multi-master]] for a ledger. :::deep - single-primary: simple, no write conflicts, but bottleneck + SPOF → needs automatic failover (Patroni/Orchestrator/RDS Multi-AZ) with the risk of [[r:split-brain]] (two primaries) if fencing is weak → needs quorum/STONITH - multi-master: writes in multiple places (low latency across regions) but must resolve *write conflicts* (LWW loses data, CRDT works for mergeable types, or the app resolves it) Fintech/OTA: a ledger is almost never multi-master; multi-region is usually single-primary-per-region + partitioned by region (data residency) + replicated reads. Active-active is reserved for data that tolerates eventual consistency (catalog, session). :::

items.q: What's the difference between partitioning and sharding? How do you choose a shard key?
items.a: - [[b:Partitioning]]: splits 1 table into multiple partitions within the *same DB* (range/hash/list) → partition pruning, managing old data - [[b:Sharding]]: splits data across *multiple independent nodes* → scales writes & storage beyond a single machine [[g:A good shard key]]: high cardinality, evenly distributed (avoids hotspots), matches the primary query pattern. Fintech typically shards by `account_id` so one user's transactions stay on the same shard (no cross-shard). :::deep Three concepts that often get asked together: - [[b:Partition]] = splitting a table within 1 node (range by month for `booking` to prune + drop old partitions fast) - [[b:Sharding]] = splitting across multiple nodes (by `user_id`) - [[b:Composite index]] = a multi-column index serving a query pattern (not splitting data) A table can *both* be range-partitioned *and* have a composite index within each partition. [[r:Shard trap]]: using `flight_id` as the shard key → hotspot on popular flights; `user_id` distributes evenly but 'all bookings for one flight' becomes scatter-gather. Bottom line: the shard key follows the *hottest query*, accepting a trade-off for secondary queries (push them to a separate read model). :::

items.q: Why is resharding painful? How does consistent hashing help?
items.a: Resharding has to move data + change the mapping while the system is running. [[g:Consistent hashing]]: maps keys & nodes onto a hash ring. - adding/removing a node only remaps a small fraction of keys (instead of nearly all of them with modulo) - [[g:virtual nodes]] help balance the load Tip: over-provision many 'logical shards' up front so scaling out later is easy. :::warn What you lose when you shard Cross-shard JOIN/transaction, global AUTO_INCREMENT, aggregation requires scatter-gather. [[r:Don't shard early]] — optimize indexes/replicas/cache first. ::: :::deep - each physical node gets only 1 point on the ring → skewed distribution, and losing a node dumps all its load onto exactly one neighboring node - assign each node ~100–200 vnodes spread around the ring → losing a node spreads the load, adding a node 'steals' a little evenly from every node (the Cassandra/DynamoDB technique) Limitations of plain consistent hashing: - still needs *rebalancing* of data + handling replicas (replicate to the next N nodes on the ring) - if [[r:range queries]] are a core requirement → hashing destroys locality → use range sharding + a directory instead of hashing :::

items.q: Generating global IDs once you've sharded: Snowflake vs UUID?
items.a:
Sharding loses global auto-increment → you need a distributed, unique ID.
SnowflakeUUIDv4UUIDv7
Structuretimestamp+machine+seq (64-bit)random 128-bittime-ordered 128-bit
Index-friendlygood (time-sequential)poor (page splits)good
Needs coordinationmachine id + clock syncnono
:::deep - [[b:Snowflake]] 64-bit = timestamp(41b)+machine(10b)+sequence(12b) → time-sequential (B+Tree-friendly, fewer splits), sortable, ~4096 ids/ms/node; needs clock sync + handling clock-skew/leap seconds - [[b:UUIDv4]] is random (no coordination needed, but destroys locality → splits, bloats secondary indexes); [[b:UUIDv7]] is time-ordered and fixes that - or a *ticket server*/*hi-lo* scheme handing out id ranges OTA: `booking_id`/`pnr` should be time-sortable (Snowflake/UUIDv7) for good write-index behavior + convenient keyset pagination + [[o:leaking less volume information]] (avoiding strictly sequential ids so competitors can't guess booking volume). :::

items.q: Explain CAP and PACELC. Which side does fintech lean toward?
items.a:
- [[b:CAP]]: when there's a Partition you must choose Consistency or Availability (P is unavoidable)
- [[b:PACELC]]: if Partitioned, choose A/C; Else (normal operation) you still trade off Latency vs Consistency

Fintech:
- core ledger/balance = [[g:CP]] (better to refuse than get the money wrong)
- peripheral (feed, displayed history) = [[o:AP/eventual]]

:::tip Bottom line
don't answer CAP in the abstract — say explicitly 'this part is CP, that part is AP'.
:::

:::deep
- when [[b:P]]artitioned → choose A or C; [[b:E]]lse (no partition) → you still trade off Latency vs Consistency (reading the primary is strongly consistent but slower/farther away, reading a replica is fast but possibly stale)
- examples: DynamoDB = PA/EL (favors availability+latency), Spanner = PC/EC (favors consistency, pays for it in latency via TrueTime)

Fintech/OTA states this *per component*:
- ledger/balance/seat hold = [[g:CP/EC]] (better to refuse/be slow than get money wrong/double-sell)
- search/availability/feed/loyalty = [[o:AP/EL]] (fast, tolerates staleness)
:::

items.q: What is distributed consensus (Raft/Paxos) used for — at what depth do you need to know it?
items.a:
[[g:Consensus]] (Raft/Paxos): multiple nodes agree on a value/ordered log despite node failures (leader election, replicated log).

It underlies etcd, the Kafka controller (KRaft), Consul, and distributed databases.

A senior engineer needs to understand the [[o:concepts]] (quorum, leader, log replication, why an odd number of nodes) rather than implement it from scratch.

:::deep
- [[b:Raft]] (easier to understand than Paxos): leader election + replicated log + [[g:quorum]] (majority of N/2+1, hence an odd number: 3 tolerates losing 1, 5 tolerates losing 2)
- an entry commits once a majority has written it → consistent despite losing a minority
- underlies etcd (K8s), Consul, Kafka KRaft (replacing Zookeeper), CockroachDB/TiDB

- why an [[o:odd number]]: avoids ties + optimizes fault tolerance/cost
- why [[o:quorum]]: any two majorities always overlap (no two valid leaders at once)
- consensus is often 'hidden' inside infrastructure (leader election for a scheduler/distributed lock) — knowing when it's in play is enough
:::

items.q: N+1 in JPA/Hibernate — how do you detect and fix it?
items.a:
[[r:N+1]]: 1 query fetches a list of N parents → each access to a lazy association fires 1 extra query.

**Fix depending on context:**
- `JOIN FETCH`/`@EntityGraph` (deliberate eager loading)
- `default_batch_fetch_size`/`@BatchSize` (batches into IN → N/k+1)
- [[g:DTO projection]] for read-heavy screens

Don't go EAGER globally; watch out for `LazyInitializationException`.

:::deep
- detect: turn on `spring.jpa.show-sql`/Hibernate statistics, or a datasource-proxy that counts queries in dev — N+1 shows up as 'one list query → N child queries'
- fix: `JOIN FETCH`/`@EntityGraph`, `@BatchSize`/`hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size` (N+1 → N/k+1), or [[g:DTO projection]] (fetch only the needed columns)

[[r:Trap]]: `JOIN FETCH` on multiple collections at once → cartesian product bloats the result set; fetch one collection per query.

OTA: a booking list screen with segments + passengers is prone to N+1 → use projection/2 batched queries instead of repeated lazy loads.

- The same problem viewed from the application layer (batching, fetch size, statement timeout) is covered in 18.8; if the domain is separated from the JPA entity, most N+1 issues disappear along with lazy loading (12-architecture-patterns.clean-layered-building-it-for-real.q2).
:::

items.q: What is CDC (Change Data Capture) / Debezium used for?
items.a:
[[g:CDC]] reads a DB's *binlog/WAL* → emits a stream of 'data that changed' without the app needing to dual-write.

Debezium pushes into Kafka, used for:
- syncing to other systems
- updating a cache/search index
- implementing [[g:Outbox]] efficiently (reading the outbox table via binlog)

Guarantees at-least-once → consumers must be [[o:idempotent]].

:::deep
- CDC reads the *transaction log* (MySQL binlog / Postgres WAL logical decoding) → emits a stream of 'row changed' events WITHOUT the app dual-writing (solves the atomic DB↔event problem)
- Debezium → Kafka: syncs search/cache, data lake, implements Outbox (reading the outbox table via binlog instead of polling)
- at-least-once + order preserved by PK → consumers must be idempotent

[[r:Traps]]: schema changes, the initial snapshot (reading the whole table) is resource-intensive, 'tombstones' on delete.

OTA: CDC from the booking DB to update the 'seats available' search index, sync loyalty/analytics, materialize a read model — decoupling services while staying eventually consistent.
:::
